title: Idioms and Prepositions
kicker: American Diploma · ACT · English: Usage and Word Choice
summary: The right small word after capable, interested, consist, prefer and dozens more — a grouped table of 50 ACT idioms, meaning-dependent prepositions and gerund vs infinitive, with a 10-question ACT-style quiz.

blocks.text: An **idiom** is a fixed way of saying something. English decides that we are *interested **in*** something but *capable **of*** something, that we *decide **to** go* but *avoid **going***. There is no logic rule that tells you which small word is right — native speakers just know it. For students who learned English as a second language, this makes idiom questions some of the hardest on the ACT. The good news: the same few dozen combinations appear again and again. This lesson gives you the method, a large grouped table to learn, and the gerund-vs-infinitive rules.
What this question type tests

Idiom questions are usage and word-choice questions. They belong to the ACT English categories **Conventions of Standard English** (38–43% of the 40 scored English questions) and **Knowledge of Language** (18–23%), which is about precise and appropriate wording. On the page they look like any other ACT English item: a short underlined portion and four choices, usually with **NO CHANGE** first, often with no stem.

You can recognise them with a **vertical scan**: the choices are almost identical and only **one small word** changes (of / for / in / to / with / on), or the verb form after a word changes (to design / designing / of designing).
The method

items: **Find the "anchor" word** just before the preposition: the adjective, verb or noun that controls it (capable, consist, responsible, interest).
**Say each choice silently with the anchor word**, ignoring the rest of the sentence: "capable of", "capable to", "capable for". The standard pair usually stands out.
**Check what follows the preposition.** After a preposition, a verb must be in the **-ing** form: capable of **designing**, interested in **learning**, insist on **paying**.
**If two choices both sound fine, check the meaning.** Some anchors take different prepositions for different meanings (agree with a person / agree to a plan).
**If you still cannot decide, eliminate any choice that is longer or adds words** — idiom questions rarely reward extra words.

blocks.title: الإيديوم مفيهوش قاعدة… احفظه
blocks.text: الـ idiom معناه كلمتين بييجوا مع بعض دايمًا زي capable of و interested in و consist of. مفيش منطق، لازم تحفظ. في الامتحان: شيل باقي الجملة وقول الكلمة مع الحرف بس (capable of ولا capable to؟). وخلي بالك: أي فعل بعد حرف جر لازم ييجي ing زي interested in learning.
The big table: 50 common ACT idioms
Learn these in groups. The right-hand column shows the mistake students most often make.
**Group A — adjective + preposition**

rows: Life in the village is different **from** life in Cairo.

blocks.text: **Group B — verb + preposition**

rows: Heavy rain resulted **in** floods. Floods resulted **from** heavy rain.

blocks.text: **Group C — noun + preposition**

rows: the reason of / the reason is because
The reason **for** the delay was the storm. The reason is **that** the road closed.
an increase of (when naming the thing)

blocks.text: **Group D — fixed expressions and paired words**

rows: not only X and also Y
either X nor Y / neither X or Y
both X as well as Y
between X to Y / between X or Y

blocks.text: **Safe ACT choices for a few disputed idioms:** *different **from*** is always correct (avoid *different than* in ACT essays); *regard X **as** Y* (not *regard X to be Y*); *independent **of***.
When the preposition changes the meaning
For some anchor words, more than one preposition is standard, but each one means something different. Here the method is **meaning first**.

rows: **with** a person / an opinion · **to** a proposal · **on** a decision both sides make
I agree **with** you. They agreed **to** the plan. We agreed **on** a date.
**to** = say one thing is like another · **with** = examine similarities and differences (careful writing keeps this difference)
She compared the city **to** a beehive. We compared this year's results **with** last year's.
**from** = be unlike · **with** = disagree with a person
My answer differs **from** yours. I differ **with** you on this point.
Smoking results **in** illness. Illness results **from** smoking.

blocks.text: Gerund or infinitive?

A **gerund** is verb + -ing used as a noun (swimming, designing). An **infinitive** is *to* + verb (to swim, to design). Some verbs must be followed by one form, some by the other. The ACT tests the most common ones.

rows: decide, plan, hope, expect, want, intend
enjoy, avoid, finish, keep, mind, quit
manage, fail, attempt, try, tend, seem
admit, deny, delay, postpone, practise, miss
✓ They **decided to build** a bridge. ✗ decided building

items: **After any preposition → -ing:** ✓ interested **in learning**, ✓ capable **of designing**, ✓ before **leaving**, ✓ instead **of waiting**. ✗ interested in to learn.

**"to" can be a preposition, not part of an infinitive.** Then it is followed by -ing: ✓ look forward **to seeing** you, ✓ be used **to working** late, ✓ object **to paying**, ✓ committed / dedicated **to protecting**, ✓ the key **to solving**. ✗ look forward to see you. **Test:** if you can put a noun after *to* (look forward to **the holiday**), *to* is a preposition → use -ing.

**Verbs that change meaning:** *stop* — ✓ He stopped **smoking** (quit) / He stopped **to smoke** (paused in order to smoke). *remember / forget* — ✓ I remember **locking** the door (I did it earlier) / Remember **to lock** the door (a task for later).
**Parallelism after these verbs:** keep both items in the same form: ✓ She enjoys **reading** and **writing**. ✗ She enjoys reading and to write.

blocks.title: to ولا ing؟
blocks.text: أفعال زي decide و plan و hope و agree و refuse و manage بعدها to + فعل: decided to build. وأفعال زي enjoy و avoid و finish و consider و suggest بعدها ing: avoided answering. وأي حرف جر (in, of, on, for) بعده ing. خلي بالك من look forward to و be used to: الـ to هنا حرف جر، فنقول look forward to seeing.
Worked examples
Each example is a sentence from an ACT-style essay. The underlined portion is shown in **bold**.
**Worked example 1 — adjective + preposition.** "Many young architects in Egypt are **capable to design** buildings that stay cool without air conditioning."
**Question:** Choose the best version of the underlined portion. If the original is best, choose NO CHANGE.

items: A) NO CHANGE
B) capable in designing
C) capable of designing
D) capable for design

blocks.text: **Answer: C.**

items: **C is correct.** The idiom is *capable **of***, and a verb after a preposition takes **-ing**: capable of designing.
**A** uses *to* + verb. **Trap:** *able to design* is correct, so *capable to design* sounds possible — but *capable* needs *of*.
**B** uses the wrong preposition.
**D** uses the wrong preposition and the bare verb *design*.

blocks.text: **Worked example 2 — verb + preposition.** "Traditional Nubian houses consist **from** thick mud-brick walls, domed roofs and a wide inner courtyard."
**Question:** Choose the best version of the underlined portion. If the original is best, choose NO CHANGE.

items: A) NO CHANGE
B) of
C) in
D) with

blocks.text: **Answer: B.**

items: **B is correct.** The idiom is *consist **of*** (= be made of).
**A** *consist from* is a common translation error.
**C** *consist in* is a rare formal idiom meaning *have as its main quality* ("Happiness consists in…"); it does not mean *be made of*. **Trap:** a real phrase with the wrong meaning.
**D** *consist with* is not standard.

blocks.text: **Worked example 3 — gerund after a verb.** "After weeks of debate, the council finally agreed **building** a footbridge across the canal."
**Question:** Choose the best version of the underlined portion. If the original is best, choose NO CHANGE.

items: A) NO CHANGE
B) on building
C) to build
D) for building

blocks.text: **Answer: C.**

items: **C is correct.** *Agree* is followed by the infinitive when you agree to do an action: agreed **to build**.
**A** uses a gerund after *agree*, which is not standard.
**B** *agree on* is used with a noun for a shared decision (agreed on a date), not with an action they will do.
**D** *agree for* is not standard.

blocks.text: **Worked example 4 — "to" as a preposition.** "The students are looking forward to **visit** the science museum in Alexandria next month."
**Question:** Choose the best version of the underlined portion. If the original is best, choose NO CHANGE.

items: A) NO CHANGE
B) visiting
C) have visited
D) be visiting

blocks.text: **Answer: B.**

items: **B is correct.** In *look forward to*, *to* is a preposition (you can say *look forward to the trip*), so the verb takes **-ing**: looking forward to visiting.
**A** treats *to* as part of an infinitive. **Trap:** this is the most common error with *look forward to*.
**C** and **D** are verb phrases that cannot follow a preposition.

blocks.text: **Worked example 5 — meaning-dependent idiom.** "At the public meeting, most residents agreed **to** the mayor that the old market should be restored rather than demolished."
**Question:** Choose the best version of the underlined portion. If the original is best, choose NO CHANGE.

items: A) NO CHANGE
B) with
C) on
D) for

blocks.text: **Answer: B.**

items: **B is correct.** You agree **with** a person or an opinion. Here the residents share the mayor's opinion, so *agreed with the mayor*.
**A** *agree to* is used for accepting a proposal or a request (agreed to the plan), not a person. **Trap:** a real idiom with the wrong meaning.
**C** *agree on* is used when people reach a shared decision about something (agreed on a date).
**D** *agree for* is not standard.

blocks.title: Classic traps
items: **The translation trap:** consist from, interested about, responsible of, depend of — these follow Arabic patterns, not English.
**capable to / succeed to / insist to:** these three need a preposition + -ing (capable of doing, succeed in doing, insist on doing).
**prefer … than:** the standard is prefer X **to** Y.
**to + base verb after a preposition-to:** look forward to see, used to work (meaning accustomed) → look forward to seeing, used to working.
**Gerund vs infinitive:** decided building, avoided to answer → decided to build, avoided answering.
**Right word, wrong meaning:** consist in, compare to, agree on — real idioms that do not fit the sentence.
**Broken pairs:** not only … and also, neither … or, between … to.

blocks.title: Fast strategy for test day
items: Only the small word changes? Say the anchor word + each preposition alone.
A verb after a preposition is always -ing.
If *to* can be followed by a noun (look forward to the trip), it is a preposition → -ing.
Check pairs: not only / but also, either / or, neither / nor, between / and, as / as.
Two choices both sound right? Decide by meaning (agree with a person, to a plan).
Before test day, read the four tables on this page aloud three times — hearing the pairs is the fastest way to learn them.

blocks.text: Practice
Two short ACT-style essays with 5 questions each. The numbers in brackets match the question numbers. Every question tests idioms, prepositions or gerund/infinitive choices.

blocks.title: Idioms and Prepositions — ACT-style practice
blocks.intro: Two ACT-style essays, 10 questions. Choose the best version of each underlined portion; NO CHANGE keeps the original. Explanations appear after you answer.

questions.p:
Farming on the Roof

In some crowded neighbourhoods of Cairo, families have turned their rooftops into small farms. A typical rooftop garden consists __from__ [1] a few wooden boxes, a water tank and a simple system of plastic pipes. Residents who are interested __in__ [2] growing their own food can learn the method in a short weekend course.

The gardens have become popular because they are __capable to produce__ [3] fresh vegetables for most of the year. Many growers prefer tomatoes and peppers __than__ [4] other crops, since these plants need little space and plenty of sun. A few families even succeed __to sell__ [5] their extra herbs to neighbours, earning a small but welcome income. The roofs also stay cooler in summer, which makes the flats below more comfortable.
questions.q: [1] Choose the best version of the underlined portion. If the original is best, choose NO CHANGE.
questions.e: The idiom is *consist **of*** (= be made of). A, B and D are not standard with *consist* in this meaning.

questions.p:
Learning the Oud

When I was fourteen, I decided __learning__ [6] the oud, the pear-shaped instrument my grandfather used to play every evening. At first the strings hurt my fingers, and I avoided __to play__ [7] the long, boring scales my teacher gave me.

My teacher was patient but strict. She insisted __on__ [8] checking my hand position at the start of every lesson, and slowly my playing improved. Now, three years later, I can play several of the songs I heard as a child, and I am looking forward __to perform__ [9] at the school's spring concert.

My grandfather did not live to hear me play, but I think he would have been proud. He always regarded music __to be__ [10] the finest gift one generation could give to the next.
questions.q: [6] Choose the best version of the underlined portion. If the original is best, choose NO CHANGE.
questions.e: *Decide* is followed by the infinitive: decided **to learn**. A uses a gerund; C and D are not standard.

blocks.title: Remember
items: Find the anchor word and say it with each preposition: capable of, interested in, consist of, responsible for, depend on, different from.
prefer X **to** Y; regard X **as** Y; not only … **but also**; neither … **nor**.
After a preposition, use -ing — including *look forward to*, *be used to*, *object to*.
decide/agree/plan/refuse/manage **to** do; enjoy/avoid/finish/consider/suggest do**ing**.
When two prepositions are both real, the meaning decides (agree with / to / on; compare to / with).
